s: The murder of Laius is identified as the pollution afflicting Thebes. Oedipus promises to investigate it as though Laius were his father and to avenge the crime.

l: Laius’s murderers, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, OEDIPUS THE KING
s: Laius’s murderers are unknown, though a surviving traveler reported that robbers attacked and killed Laius. Oedipus orders anyone who knows their identity to speak and threatens the murderers with banishment or worse.

l: blood-guiltiness, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, OEDIPUS THE KING
s: Blood-guiltiness is presented as the cause of Thebes’s suffering and must be purged according to Apollo’s command. Oedipus declares that the guilty person must be expelled or punished so that the land can be cleansed.

l: the riddle of the Sphinx, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, OEDIPUS THE KING
s: The riddle of the Sphinx once prevented Thebes from pursuing the older mystery of Laius’s death. Oedipus claims that he solved it by his own intelligence rather than through prophetic signs.

l: the State, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, OEDIPUS THE KING
s: The plague-stricken city is filled with corpses, mourning, failed crops, dying animals, and women suffering in childbirth. Its inhabitants gather at altars and ask Oedipus and the gods for deliverance.

l: the oracle’s banishment, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, OEDIPUS THE KING
s: The oracle’s prescribed banishment is one possible expiation for the pollution caused by Laius’s murder. Oedipus adopts it in his proclamation, promising that the murderer may leave Thebes without suffering the capital charge.

l: the gods, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, OEDIPUS THE KING
s: The gods are invoked as the powers who sent the oracle and may save Thebes from plague. The Chorus calls upon Zeus, Apollo, Athena, Artemis, Ares, and Dionysus for protection and healing.

l: Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus urges Oedipus and Teiresias to stop quarreling and consider how to fulfill the oracle. Teiresias declares that Oedipus does not know his lineage and is unknowingly an enemy to his living and dead kin. He prophesies that Oedipus will be driven into exile, lose his sight, and discover that he is the murderer of Laius, the brother and husband of his mother, and the father and half-brother of his children. Oedipus angrily rejects Teiresias, who then leaves after delivering the prophecy.

l: Chorus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus says that both Teiresias and Oedipus have spoken angrily and urges them to stop quarreling and determine how best to fulfill the oracle.

l: Oedipus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: Oedipus angrily insults Teiresias and orders him to leave. Teiresias declares that Oedipus does not know his lineage and prophesies that he will be exposed as the murderer of Laius, the husband and son of his mother, and the brother and father of his children.

l: Teiresias, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: Teiresias claims the right to speak freely and says that he serves Loxias rather than Creon. He tells Oedipus that he is unknowingly hostile to his own kin, then prophesies his loss of sight, exile, and discovery of his connection to Laius's murder and his family.

l: Oedipus's biological parents, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: Teiresias says that Oedipus does not know the parents who begat him. He states that Oedipus is an unwitting enemy to both his living and dead kin.

l: Jocasta, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: Teiresias says that Oedipus's mother bore him a son who is also her husband. He further prophesies that Oedipus will be proven her son and husband, and the brother of her children.

l: the oracle, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus refers to an oracle and urges consultation about how best to fulfill it.

l: curse of Oedipus's mother and father, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: Teiresias says that the curse of Oedipus's mother and father will one day drive him beyond the borders.

l: Oedipus's blindness, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: Teiresias says that Oedipus's eyes currently see clearly but will thereafter be plunged into endless night. He also describes Oedipus as becoming blind of seeing and moving in beggar's clothing with a staff.

l: the murder of Laius, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: Teiresias identifies the man whom Oedipus has sought to arrest for murdering Laius as present in Thebes. He says that this man will be shown to be a native-born Theban and will be revealed as Laius's assassin.

l: Oedipus's birth, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: Teiresias says that the day will be Oedipus's birth-day and his grave. He also refers to the strange circumstances of the hymeneal with which Oedipus was borne home.

l: Oedipus’s marriage to Jocasta, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: Teiresias prophesies that Oedipus will discover that his marriage made him the husband of the woman who bore him. He describes him as her son and husband both.

l: Oedipus's exile, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: Teiresias prophesies that the curse of Oedipus's mother and father will drive him beyond the borders. He says Oedipus will grope his way toward a strange land.

l: Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus describes the unnamed doer of a murder as pursued by Apollo and the Fates after a command from Parnassus to discover him. It expresses uncertainty about the master seer’s words and says it knows of no old or recent quarrel between the Labdacidan house and the ruler, Polybus’ son. The Chorus honors Zeus and Apollo but questions whether a mortal seer has proved superior to others in knowledge. It also struggles to accept that a crime has been committed by Oedipus, who once saved the State from the winged songstress.

l: Chorus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus describes the doer of the murder as fleeing under pursuit by Apollo and the Fates. It is perplexed by the master seer’s words, knows of no feud involving the Labdacidan house and the ruler, Polybus’ son, and cannot accept the charge laid against Oedipus without proof.

l: Apollo, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: Apollo is associated with the lightnings of his Sire and pursues the doer of the murder as the avenging Phoebus. The Chorus calls Apollo wise and says that nothing is hidden from him.

l: Teiresias, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: The master seer’s words perplex the Chorus, which does not know whether they are true or false. The Chorus questions whether a mortal seer has ever proved that he knows more than others or can accuse someone without assured signs.

l: murder, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: A summons orders that the undiscovered doer of the murder be sought near and far. The Chorus says it has no proof sufficient to challenge the ruler’s good name or join in a blood-feud over the deed.

l: doer of the murder, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: The doer of the murder is described as responsible for foul deeds and bloodshed. He roams like a sullen bull, tries vainly to escape his doom, and is pursued by Apollo and the Fates.

l: Labdacidan house, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus says it knows of no quarrel, either ancient or recent, between the Labdacidan house and the ruler, Polybus’ son.

l: Oedipus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: A crime is laid against Oedipus, but the Chorus cannot assent to the accusation without proof. It recalls that he saved the State when the winged songstress came.

l: winged songstress, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: The winged songstress came to the State and was tested and tried before everyone. Oedipus is credited with saving the State in connection with her appearance.

l: the murder of Laius, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: A crime is laid on Oedipus, but the Chorus asks how it can assent to the charge without proof.

l: oracle’s voice, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: The oracle’s voice is presented as a divine voice from Earth’s mid shrine. It issues the summons to seek near and far for the undiscovered doer of the murder.

l: Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: Creon defends himself against Oedipus’s accusation that he conspired with the seer to seize the throne, arguing that he prefers influence and security to kingship; Jocasta and the Chorus stop the quarrel, and Oedipus reluctantly lets him go. Jocasta recounts that Laius was supposedly killed by robbers at a crossroads and that his infant son was exposed, while Oedipus realizes that he may have killed Laius during an encounter at branching roads. Oedipus explains that Apollo’s prophecy said he would kill his father and marry his mother, and he orders the surviving herdsman brought to Thebes to confirm whether Laius was killed by one man or by robbers. The Chorus prays for reverence toward divine law and laments that faith in Apollo and the oracle has weakened.

l: Oedipus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: Oedipus accuses Creon of plotting against him and of using the seer as a mouthpiece. After hearing Jocasta’s account of Laius’s death and comparing it with his own encounter at the crossroads, he fears that he killed Laius and asks that the surviving herdsman be brought to him.

l: Creon, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: Creon denies conspiring against Oedipus and argues that he has no desire to be king because he already enjoys influence and security through Oedipus. He offers to have his account tested at Delphi and is allowed to leave after Jocasta and the Chorus intervene.

l: Jocasta, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: Jocasta tries to reconcile Oedipus and Creon and urges Oedipus to trust Creon’s oath. She recounts the prophecy given to Laius, the reported murder at a place where three roads meet, and the exposure of Laius’s infant son; after hearing Oedipus’s story, she agrees to summon the surviving herdsman.

l: Chorus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: The Chorus attempts to calm the quarrel between Oedipus and Creon and asks Oedipus not to condemn Creon on suspicion. It later praises divine law, condemns insolence and impiety, and laments that Apollo and the oracle are no longer heeded.

l: Laius, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: Laius was said to have been murdered by robbers at a place where roads from Delphi and Daulis meet. Jocasta describes him as tall, lightly silver-haired, and similar in form to Oedipus; Oedipus suspects that the man he killed at the crossroads was Laius.

l: Polybus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: Polybus is identified by Oedipus as his father, who ruled or lived in Corinth and raised him.

l: Merope, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: Merope is identified by Oedipus as his mother and as a Dorian.

l: Apollo, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: Apollo sent Oedipus back from Delphi without the information he sought but gave him prophecies that he would defile his mother’s bed, raise abhorrent offspring, and kill the father from whose loins he sprang. The Chorus invokes Apollo and laments that faith in him has declined.

l: Teiresias, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: The seer had a high reputation and had previously been consulted about Laius’s murder, but he did not identify Oedipus at that time. Oedipus claims that Creon prompted the seer to accuse him of killing Laius.

l: the surviving herdsman, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: The surviving herdsman, described as a serf or bondsman, was the sole survivor who returned after Laius’s death and reported what happened. Jocasta had sent him away to the mountain pastures, and Oedipus orders that he be brought back for questioning.

l: Thebes, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: Thebes is ruled by Oedipus after Laius’s death, and its people are distressed by the conflict between Oedipus and Creon. The city heard the initial report that Laius was killed by robbers.

l: Delphi, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: Delphi is the place Oedipus visited to seek knowledge about his parentage and received Apollo’s prophecies instead. Creon proposes that Oedipus go to Delphi to verify whether Creon reported the god’s answer truthfully.

l: the crossroads, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: The crossroads, where branches from Delphi and Daulis meet, is identified as the place where Laius was reportedly murdered. Oedipus recalls encountering and killing an older man and his attendants at a place with three branching roads.

l: the State, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: The State of Thebes is described as stricken and vulnerable to further harm if discord continues between Oedipus and Creon. The Chorus regards Oedipus as the leader who previously brought the distracted State to a quiet haven.

l: the oracle concerning Laius, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: The oracle concerning Laius declared that Laius would perish by the hand of his own son. Jocasta says Laius’s infant son was exposed and that the prophecy did not come true because the child supposedly died before killing him.

l: prophecy, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: The prophecy of Oedipus’s fate said that he would defile his mother’s bed, father abhorrent children, and kill the father who raised him. Oedipus fears that his encounter at the crossroads may have fulfilled part of it.

l: the murder of Laius, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: Laius’s murder was reported as an attack by robbers at a crossroads, with Laius riding in a mule-car and accompanied by five attendants. Oedipus recounts killing an old man and the others during a road confrontation and wonders whether the old man was Laius.

l: the quarrel between Oedipus and Creon, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: The quarrel between Oedipus and Creon begins when Oedipus accuses Creon of arranging the seer’s charge and plotting to take the crown. Jocasta and the Chorus intervene, after which Oedipus allows Creon to leave despite continuing to hate and suspect him.

l: Oedipus's exile, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: Oedipus considers exile one possible consequence if he is guilty of Laius’s murder and the other crimes foretold by the prophecy. He imagines being banished from his native land and separated from those he loves.

l: Antigone’s family curse, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: Oedipus recognizes that he has pronounced a dreadful curse against himself after hearing that Laius was killed at a place where three roads meet. He says that the curse would make him unclean and subject to banishment if he is Laius’s killer.

l: Oedipus's alleged crimes, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: Oedipus’s alleged crimes are killing Laius, defiling the bed of the man he killed, marrying his own mother, and killing his father. He fears that the first of these may already have occurred and that the rest may follow the prophecy.

l: the plague afflicting Thebes, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CREON.
s: The plague afflicting Thebes is reflected in the statement that the whole land lies stricken and that the State is distracted and in distress. The Chorus fears that continued discord between Oedipus and Creon will worsen the city’s suffering.

l: Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter JOCASTA.]
s: Jocasta tells Oedipus that Polybus has died naturally, apparently disproving the oracle that Oedipus would kill his father. The Corinthian Messenger then reveals that Polybus was not Oedipus’s biological father and that Oedipus was given to him as an infant by Laius’s Herdsman. The Herdsman admits that the child was Laius’s son, born to Jocasta, and was exposed because of a prophecy that he would kill his father. Oedipus realizes that he has fulfilled the prophecies through parricide and marriage to his mother, while Jocasta leaves in anguish.

l: Oedipus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter JOCASTA.]
s: Oedipus hears that Polybus has died and briefly believes the prophecies about killing his father have failed. He learns from the Corinthian Messenger and Laius’s Herdsman that he is not Polybus’s biological son but the child of Laius and Jocasta. He recognizes that he has killed his father and married his mother, then leaves in horror.

l: Jocasta, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter JOCASTA.]
s: Jocasta brings offerings to Apollo because Oedipus is distressed by ominous predictions. She rejoices at Polybus’s death, believing it disproves the prophecy, but becomes alarmed when Oedipus investigates his birth. After the Herdsman confirms that she gave him the infant, she leaves, declaring that she will remain silent.

l: Corinthian Messenger, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter JOCASTA.]
s: The Corinthian Messenger reports that Polybus is dead and that the people of Corinth have decided to make Oedipus king. He tells Oedipus that Polybus was not his biological father and that he received Oedipus as a child from Laius’s Herdsman after finding him on Cithaeron.

l: the surviving herdsman, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter JOCASTA.]
s: Laius’s Herdsman confirms that he tended sheep for Laius on Cithaeron. He admits that he received Laius’s child from within Laius’s household and gave the infant to the Corinthian Messenger. He says the child was intended to be destroyed because of the prophecy that he would kill his father, but that he spared him out of pity.

l: Polybus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter JOCASTA.]
s: Polybus, who was regarded as Oedipus’s father and king of Corinth, dies naturally after reaching old age. His death leads Oedipus and Jocasta to think that the oracle concerning Oedipus’s parricide has failed, but the Messenger later reveals that Polybus was not Oedipus’s biological father.

l: Laius, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter JOCASTA.]
s: Laius is identified as the former king whose household included the Herdsman and whose child was given away. The Herdsman confirms that the infant was Laius’s own son and that the child was exposed because of a prophecy that he would kill Laius.

l: Chorus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter JOCASTA.]
s: The Chorus observes Jocasta’s distress and encourages the search for the Herdsman. After Oedipus learns the truth, it sings of his fall from power and happiness, declaring that his birth and marriage have brought together son and father in one bed.

l: Corinth, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter JOCASTA.]
s: Corinth is the city from which the Messenger comes and where Polybus had been king. Its people have reportedly resolved to make Oedipus king after Polybus’s death.

l: Thebes, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter JOCASTA.]
s: The text presents Thebes through its royal household and elders, who witness the discovery of Oedipus’s birth and the fulfillment of the prophecies. The Chorus recalls that Oedipus had been honored as the city’s savior and king.

l: Cithaeron, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter JOCASTA.]
s: Cithaeron is the mountain region where Laius’s Herdsman tended flocks and where the infant Oedipus was found. The Chorus calls it the nurse and foster-mother of Oedipus.

l: oracle, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter JOCASTA.]
s: The oracle had foretold that Oedipus would kill his father and marry his mother. Jocasta and Oedipus initially think the oracle has been disproved by Polybus’s natural death, but the later revelation shows that its words have been fulfilled.

l: Antigone’s family curse, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter JOCASTA.]
s: Jocasta prays for Apollo to cleanse the land from its curse. Oedipus ultimately describes himself as cursed in birth, marriage, and parricide after learning the truth about his identity.

l: prophecy, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter JOCASTA.]
s: The prophecy states that Oedipus will shed the blood of his father and marry his mother. The revelation that Laius was his father and Jocasta his mother shows that the prophecy has come to pass.

l: death of Polybus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter JOCASTA.]
s: The Corinthian Messenger announces that Polybus has died naturally after living through the full span of his years. His death initially reassures Jocasta and Oedipus, but it is later shown not to disprove the prophecy because Polybus was not Oedipus’s biological father.

l: Oedipus’s birth revelation, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter JOCASTA.]
s: The Corinthian Messenger and Laius’s Herdsman reveal that Oedipus was born to Laius and Jocasta, exposed as an infant, and given to the Messenger. Oedipus learns that Polybus and Merope were not his biological parents.

l: Oedipus’s marriage to Jocasta, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter JOCASTA.]
s: Oedipus’s marriage to Jocasta is revealed to be a marriage to his biological mother. Jocasta realizes the truth before Oedipus and leaves in anguish, while the Chorus condemns the marriage bed that served for both son and father.

l: parricide, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter JOCASTA.]
s: Oedipus had feared that he would kill his father, but he believed Polybus’s death without his involvement disproved the prediction. After learning that Laius was his biological father, he recognizes that his killing of Laius was the foretold parricide.

l: Oedipus’s abandonment as an infant, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter JOCASTA.]
s: Oedipus was given to Laius’s Herdsman as an infant so that he could be destroyed because of the prophecy concerning his future. The Herdsman spared him out of pity and passed him to the Corinthian Messenger, who gave him to Polybus and Merope.

l: Fate, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter JOCASTA.]
s: The Chorus presents Oedipus’s fall as the work of fate and declares that no mortal should be called blessed before life has ended. Events that seemed to defeat the prophecy instead lead to its fulfillment through Oedipus’s birth, parricide, and marriage.

l: Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter SECOND MESSENGER.]
s: The Second Messenger reports that Jocasta has died by hanging and that Oedipus blinded himself after discovering the truth about his marriage and his crimes. Oedipus laments that he murdered Laius, married his mother, and brought ruin upon the house of Labdacus, and he begs to be removed from Thebes. Creon assumes guardianship, agrees to care for Jocasta’s burial and Oedipus’s daughters, but says the gods must be consulted about exile. Antigone and Ismene are brought to Oedipus, who mourns the suffering and disgrace they may face, while the Chorus warns that no mortal should be called happy before the end of life.

l: Second Messenger, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter SECOND MESSENGER.]
s: The Second Messenger tells the Chorus that Jocasta is dead and describes how she hanged herself in the bridal chamber. He then recounts Oedipus’s discovery of her body, his self-blinding, and his desire to be exiled.

l: Chorus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter SECOND MESSENGER.]
s: The Chorus reacts with grief and horror to Jocasta’s death and Oedipus’s blinding. It questions Oedipus, condemns the dreadful condition of his life, and concludes that no one should be considered happy until life has ended.

l: Thebes, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter SECOND MESSENGER.]
s: Thebes is the city Oedipus once ruled and from which he asks to be expelled. Oedipus says he cannot remain in the city of his sires after being declared unclean.
